tagline: The dark years between Joshua and the kings, when Israel kept forgetting God and God kept raising up flawed deliverers to rescue them.
overview:
Judges tells what happened to Israel after Joshua died and before there was a king. The tribes have entered Canaan, but they have not finished taking the land, and the book opens with the unfinished work: Canaanite cities left standing, peoples left in place, and a generation that grows up not knowing the LORD or what he had done. From there the book settles into a pattern it announces in chapter 2. Israel does evil and serves other gods, God hands them over to an oppressor, they cry out, and God raises up a judge, a military and tribal leader, who rescues them. Then the judge dies and the whole thing starts again, a little worse each time.

The judges themselves are unforgettable and uncomfortable: Othniel, the model deliverer; Ehud, the left-handed assassin; Deborah, the prophet who judges Israel under a palm tree, and Jael, who kills a fleeing general with a tent peg; Gideon, the frightened farmer who becomes a hero and then makes an idol; Abimelech, his son, who murders seventy brothers to become a king; Jephthah, the outcast whose rash vow costs his daughter; and Samson, the strongest man in Israel and one of its weakest. The last five chapters leave the judges behind altogether and show a household idol, a tribe stealing a priest, a Levite's concubine abused and dismembered, and a civil war that nearly wipes out the tribe of Benjamin.

The book matters because it is honest. It doesn't pretend God's people are better than they are, and it doesn't pretend that God abandons them. Its repeated line near the end, that in those days there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes, diagnoses a people who have lost their center. Judges is a mirror for any community that has inherited faith without knowing the God behind it, and it is a testimony to a God whose patience outlasts his people's forgetting.
author:
The book doesn't name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 14b), credits it to Samuel, the prophet who stands at the turn from the judges to the kings. The book's repeated comment that there was no king in Israel at that time suggests a writer who knew the monarchy and looked back on the earlier period from it.

Many modern scholars read Judges as part of a larger work running from Deuteronomy through 2 Kings, often called the Deuteronomistic History (a theory proposed by Martin Noth in 1943), which interprets Israel's story through the covenant terms of Deuteronomy: faithfulness brings blessing and idolatry brings loss of the land. On this view, older hero stories and poems (such as the Song of Deborah in chapter 5, widely regarded as one of the oldest pieces of Hebrew poetry) were gathered and framed by later editors. Others hold that the book was composed much closer to the events, early in the monarchy, from reliable earlier sources. Both views agree that the book as we have it is a deliberate, carefully shaped work rather than a loose collection.
date:
Two dates matter: the period the book describes and the time it was written. The period runs from the death of Joshua to the eve of Samuel and Saul. Those who date the exodus to the fifteenth century BC place the judges roughly between 1375 and 1050 BC; those who date it to the thirteenth century place them roughly between 1200 and 1050 BC. The book's own numbers (its years of oppression and rest) add up to more time than either scheme allows if read end to end, and many readers conclude that some judges were regional leaders whose careers overlapped.

For the writing, the refrain about there being no king points to a time when kingship existed, and the notice in 18:30 that a priestly line served at Dan until the land went into captivity suggests at least that verse was written after an exile, probably the Assyrian deportations of the eighth century BC. Scholars who hold to early composition date most of the book to the early monarchy, around the time of Saul or David; others place its final edition in the late monarchy or the Babylonian exile in the sixth century BC.
setting:
The world of Judges is the land of Canaan in the early Iron Age, after the widespread collapse of the great Late Bronze Age powers around 1200 BC. Egypt's hold on Canaan was weakening, and no empire controlled the region. The Egyptian Merneptah Stele, from about 1208 BC, already mentions a people called Israel in Canaan. Into that vacuum came local powers: Canaanite city-kings with chariots in the northern valleys, Moabites and Ammonites east of the Jordan, Midianite and Amalekite raiders on camels from the desert, and, most dangerous of all, the Philistines, one of the so-called Sea Peoples, who settled on the southern coast in the twelfth century BC and dominate the Samson stories.

Israel had no capital, no standing army, and no central government. It was a loose confederation of tribes, each settled in its own region, bound together by kinship and by covenant with the LORD, and with a shared sanctuary at Shiloh. Most Israelites lived in small hill-country villages, farming grain, olives, and grapes and herding sheep and goats. Their neighbors worshiped Baal, the storm god who was believed to bring rain and fertility, and goddesses such as Asherah and Astarte. For a farming people whose lives depended on rain, the pull of those gods was constant and practical.
purpose: Judges was written for Israel, to explain how a people who had received the land under Joshua fell into chaos, and to call them back to the covenant. It shows what happens when a generation doesn't know the LORD: spiritual forgetting becomes moral collapse, and moral collapse becomes social violence. It also prepares for the monarchy. The refrain that there was no king in Israel invites the reader to long for a king who will lead the people in faithfulness, while the stories of Gideon's refusal of kingship and Abimelech's bloody grab for it warn that a bad king is no answer. Underneath the whole book runs the question of who really rules Israel, and the answer the book keeps giving is that the LORD does, even when no one acknowledges it.
story: Judges follows Joshua, which ends with the land allotted, the covenant renewed at Shechem, and a warning that Israel would not find faithfulness easy. Judges shows that warning coming true. It is followed in the English Bible by Ruth, a quiet story set in the days when the judges ruled that ends with the genealogy of David, and then by 1 and 2 Samuel, where the last judge, Samuel, anoints Israel's first kings. In the Hebrew Bible, Judges belongs to the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings), which tell Israel's history as a prophetic account of God's dealings with his people.
christ: Judges is full of saviors who can't save for long. Each judge brings rest to the land, and each rest ends when the judge dies. Several of them are deeply flawed, and the Spirit of the LORD comes on people who go on to make terrible choices. The book leaves its reader longing for a deliverer who will not die and leave the people to relapse, and for a king who will do what is right in God's eyes rather than his own. The New Testament names some of the judges (Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah) among those who acted by faith (Hebrews 11:32), not because their lives were clean but because they trusted God in weakness. Christians have seen in the whole pattern of the book a picture of the human need that Jesus meets: a savior raised up by God, anointed by the Spirit, who wins deliverance through his own death and then lives forever. That link is thematic rather than predictive; Judges doesn't foretell Christ, but it shows why a better deliverer and a better king were needed.
reading:
Judges is narrative history with poetry woven in, and it rarely stops to tell you what to think. The narrator often lets a story's ugliness speak for itself, so a reader should not assume that everything a judge does is approved simply because it is recorded. Watch the framework: the repeated phrases (Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD, the land had rest, the Spirit of the LORD came upon him) are the book's commentary. Watch the downward slope as well. The early judges are relatively admirable; the later ones are compromised; and by the end the Levites, who should guard Israel's worship, are part of the rot. The treatment of women is a useful barometer: the book moves from Achsah, who asks for and receives a blessing, and Deborah, who leads, to Jephthah's daughter and the Levite's concubine, who are sacrificed and destroyed.

A common misreading turns the judges into moral heroes to imitate. Another reads the book as nothing but grim violence. Better to read it as the book reads itself: a sober account of how God stayed faithful to a people who kept breaking faith, and a warning to every generation that inherits a faith it has not made its own.

structure.title: An unfinished conquest
structure.summary: After Joshua's death the tribes fight for their territories with mixed success, leaving many Canaanites in the land. The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bokim.

structure.title: The pattern announced
structure.summary: A new generation forgets the LORD, and the narrator sets out the cycle of sin, oppression, crying out, and deliverance that shapes the book.

structure.title: The earlier judges
structure.summary: Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar, Deborah and Barak, and Gideon deliver Israel from Aram, Moab, the Philistines, Canaan, and Midian, though Gideon's story ends in an idol.

structure.title: Abimelech, Jephthah, and the minor judges
structure.summary: Abimelech seizes kingship by murder and is destroyed, and Jephthah rescues Israel from Ammon at a terrible cost. Brief notices record Tola, Jair, Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon.

structure.title: Samson
structure.summary: A child promised and set apart as a Nazirite grows into a strong, self-willed man who fights the Philistines alone and dies bringing down their temple.

structure.title: No king in Israel
structure.summary: Two appendices show the collapse of worship and morals: Micah's idol and the Danite migration, and the outrage at Gibeah followed by a civil war against Benjamin.

themes.title: Forgetting and its cost
themes.body: The book's crisis begins with a generation that did not know the LORD or the work he had done for Israel (2:10). Faith was not handed down, and what filled the gap was the religion of the neighbors. Judges traces how that forgetting worked itself out: in idolatry first, then in moral confusion, and finally in violence among Israelites themselves. The book treats remembering God's acts as a matter of life and death for a community.

themes.title: The cycle and the spiral
themes.body: The pattern of sin, oppression, crying out, and rescue repeats, but it does not simply loop. Each turn goes lower. Othniel's story is brief and clean; by Gideon the judge himself leads Israel into idolatry, by Jephthah a judge kills fellow Israelites, and by Samson the judge never calls the people to anything and dies alone. The book describes a downward spiral rather than a circle, and it ends in a place worse than where it began.

themes.title: God's persistent mercy
themes.body: Again and again the LORD is moved by his people's groaning under their oppressors and raises up a deliverer, often before they have truly repented. In chapter 10 he tells them to go and cry to the gods they have chosen, and yet he cannot bear Israel's misery. Judges shows a God who judges sin in earnest and still refuses to give up on the people he has bound himself to by covenant.

themes.title: Unlikely and flawed deliverers
themes.body: God uses a left-handed man, a woman, a farmer threshing in a winepress, the son of a prostitute, and a man who breaks nearly every vow he carries. The Spirit of the LORD comes upon them for the task of rescue. The book is clear that this gift of power is not the same as good character, and several judges misuse what God has given. The deliverance is God's, carried out through very human hands.

themes.title: The question of kingship
themes.body: Who should rule Israel? Gideon refuses to be king because the LORD is Israel's ruler, then lives like one. Abimelech takes the crown by murder and brings ruin. Jotham's fable mocks a king who is only a bramble. The closing refrain, that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes, points toward the need for faithful leadership under God, and the books that follow take up that longing.

keyChapters.why: The book's key: a generation forgets the LORD, and the narrator lays out the cycle of apostasy and deliverance that the rest of the book follows.
Deborah, Barak, and Jael defeat Sisera's chariots, one of the book's clearest victories, told again in the poetry of chapter 5.
God calls fearful Gideon, patiently answers his tests, and begins to tear down the altar of Baal in Gideon's own family.
Abimelech's murderous grab for kingship and Jotham's fable show what happens when a man makes himself king without God.
Jephthah, an outcast, delivers Israel from Ammon, and his rash vow ends in one of the most painful stories in Scripture.
Samson's fall to Delilah and his death in the temple of Dagon close the stories of the judges.
The book ends in civil war and desperate improvisation, with the verdict that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

parts.body:
Judges is the seventh book of the Bible. It has 21 chapters, and it tells what happened to Israel after Joshua died and before there was a king.

The tribes are in the land, but the land is not fully theirs. Canaanite towns still stand among them, and a new generation grows up ‘who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel’ (2:10). From there the book turns like a wheel. Israel serves other gods. God gives them into the hands of an enemy. They cry out, and God raises up a deliverer, called a judge, who sets them free. When the judge dies, it all begins again, and each time it goes a little lower.

Some of the judges are among the most vivid people in the Bible: Ehud, the left-handed man with the hidden dagger; Deborah, the prophet who judged Israel under a palm tree; Gideon, the frightened farmer; Jephthah, the outcast whose vow cost him his daughter; and Samson, the strongest man in Israel and one of its weakest. Then the judges disappear, and the last five chapters tell two stories of what Israel had become.

The book gives its own verdict on those years, and it gives it twice, at the start of those last chapters and in its very last verse: “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (17:6; 21:25). That sentence frames everything else. Judges is not a gallery of heroes to copy. It is an honest account of a people coming apart, and of a God who would not give them up. Its hardest chapters are among the darkest in the Bible. These notes face them plainly, without relish and without excuse.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Judges follows straight on from Joshua. Joshua ends with an old leader renewing the covenant at Shechem and warning the people that serving God would not be easy. It ends with three graves in the promised land and a good word on that generation. Judges takes up the same scene and the same words: “And the people served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him, who had seen all the great works that the LORD had done for Israel” (2:7). Then it tells what came after.

Ahead of Judges lie the kings. In the English Bible, Ruth comes next, a quiet story set ‘In the days when the judges ruled’ (Ruth 1:1) that ends with the family line of David. Then 1 and 2 Samuel tell how Samuel, the last of the judges, anointed Israel's first kings. When the elders finally ask for one, they use the old word for what the judges did: “Give us a king to judge us” (1 Samuel 8:6).

In the Hebrew Bible, Judges is the second of the books called the Former Prophets: Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings. Together they tell Israel's story in the land from the crossing of the Jordan to the exile in Babylon, and they tell it as prophets would, measuring each generation by the covenant God made with them.

So Judges stands between two ages. Behind it are the promise to Abraham, the law of Moses and the gift of the land. Ahead of it are the kings. In between are the years when Israel had no capital, no standing army and no central government. It was a loose alliance of tribes, each settled in its own region, held together by kinship and by its covenant with the LORD, with a shared sanctuary at Shiloh.

The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 14b), credits it to Samuel, the prophet who stands at the turn from the judges to the kings.

The book itself looks back on the period from a later time. Its refrain, ‘In those days there was no king in Israel’, speaks to readers who knew a time when there was one. And one verse says that a line of priests served at Dan ‘until the day of the captivity of the land’ (18:30). Many read that as the Assyrian deportations of northern Israel, which began around 733 BC. Others think it means an earlier disaster, perhaps the Philistine capture of the ark and the loss of Shiloh in Samuel's day, which would fit the next verse.

Many modern scholars read Judges as part of a larger work running from Deuteronomy to 2 Kings, following a proposal made by the German scholar Martin Noth in 1943. On this view older hero stories and poems were gathered and framed by later editors, who read Israel's history through the covenant of Deuteronomy: faithfulness brings life in the land, and idolatry brings its loss. The Song of Deborah in chapter 5 is widely held to be one of the oldest pieces of Hebrew poetry. Others hold that the book was written much closer to the events, early in the time of the kings, from reliable earlier sources. Those who hold to an early date place most of the book around the time of Saul or David. Others place its final edition late in the time of the kings, or in the exile in Babylon in the sixth century BC.

The views agree on one thing. The book as it stands is a deliberate, carefully shaped work, and not a loose collection of tales. Christians who receive Judges as God's word hold more than one of these views, and these notes take no side among them.

parts.h: Dates, years and what has been dug up
parts.body:
When the events took place depends, as with Joshua, on the date of the exodus. Those who date the exodus to the fifteenth century BC place the judges roughly between 1375 and 1050 BC. Those who date it to the thirteenth century place them roughly between 1200 and 1050 BC. On either view the period ends with Samuel and Saul in the eleventh century BC.

The book gives numbers as it goes: eight years under Cushan-rishathaim, then forty years of rest under Othniel; eighteen under Eglon of Moab, then eighty of rest after Ehud; twenty under Jabin, then forty after Deborah; and so on to Samson's twenty years. Laid end to end, these add up to about four hundred years, more than either scheme allows. Many readers conclude that some judges were regional leaders whose careers overlapped. The book itself names two oppressions in one verse, by the Philistines and by the Ammonites (10:7), and the two may have overlapped, one from the west and one from the east. When Jephthah tells the king of Ammon that Israel had lived in the land for three hundred years (11:26), those who hold the earlier date of the exodus see support for it, and others read the figure as a round number in a speech. The chapter does not settle the question.

The world around the book is better known. Around 1200 BC the great powers of the Late Bronze Age collapsed, and Egypt's hold on Canaan weakened. A victory monument of Pharaoh Merneptah, from about 1208 BC, already names a people called Israel in Canaan. In the same centuries the central hill country filled with new villages. Surveys have found more than 250 small settlements of the early Iron Age, most of them on hilltops where few had lived before. The Israel of this book is also a people of the hills, who could not take the fortified towns of the plains (1:19, 1:27). How those villagers relate to the Bible's stories of the exodus and the conquest is one of the most argued questions in the field. Some see newcomers, some see Canaanites who moved up into the hills, and many see a mix.

The Philistines arrived in the same years. They were among the groups that Egyptian records call the Sea Peoples, and temple reliefs of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu name one group the Peleset, generally identified with the Philistines. They settled on the southern coast in five cities, and their towns show a way of life of their own, including decorated pottery with Aegean roots.

A few sites in the book have been dug. Hazor was destroyed by fire in the Late Bronze Age, and how Joshua's victory over its king relates to the Jabin of chapter 4 is debated. At Shechem excavators found a great fortress-temple, which some connect with the temple of chapter 9, though that link is also debated. At Dan they found an Iron Age city with a large platform for worship. The site's page on what archaeology shows notes that for the centuries before the ninth century BC the evidence is thinner and argued over, and that it neither proves the biblical accounts nor shows them false. The judges belong to those earlier centuries. These notes set out what has been found, and claim no more for it than it shows.

Judges has three parts, and its beginning and its end answer each other.

The opening (1:1 to 3:6) comes in two layers. Chapter 1 tells, tribe by tribe, how the land was only partly taken. Judah wins at Bezek, Hebron and Debir, but the chapter turns into a list of towns that were not taken: “At that time Manasseh failed to drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, Megiddo, and their villages” (1:27). The angel of the LORD rebukes Israel at Bochim, and the people weep (2:1-5). Then chapter 2 steps back and sets out the pattern of the whole period.

The middle (3:7 to 16:31) tells the stories of the judges: Othniel, Ehud and Shamgar; Deborah and Barak, with Jael; Gideon, and his son Abimelech, who made himself king; Tola and Jair; Jephthah; Ibzan, Elon and Abdon; and Samson. Some get a single verse and some get four chapters.

The ending (17:1 to 21:25) leaves the judges behind. It tells two stories. In the first, a man named Micah sets up a household shrine, and the tribe of Dan steals it, with its priest, on the way to destroying a quiet town (chapters 17 and 18). In the second, a woman is handed over to a crowd in the town of Gibeah, a civil war nearly wipes out the tribe of Benjamin, and young women are seized as wives for the survivors (chapters 19 to 21). Four times these chapters say that there was no king in Israel, and twice they add that everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

The opening and the ending mirror each other. The book begins with Israel asking the LORD who should go up first against the Canaanites, and the answer is Judah (1:1-2). Near its end Israel asks the same question, and Judah is sent first again, this time against their own brothers of Benjamin (20:18). And the book that began with Israel asking for the LORD's direction ends with Israel making its own plans. Its last cry to God, asking why this has happened in Israel (21:3), receives no recorded answer.

Chapter 2 is the key to the middle of the book. It describes in advance a wheel that turns again and again. ‘And the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals’ (2:11). The LORD's anger burns, he gives them into the hands of raiders, and they are ‘greatly distressed’ (2:15). Then “the LORD raised up judges, who saved them from the hands of those who plundered them” (2:16). While the judge lives, Israel is safe. “But when the judge died, the Israelites became even more corrupt than their fathers” (2:19).

Once a reader knows the wheel, the stories show its parts in the same few phrases. Israel ‘did evil in the sight of the LORD’. They ‘cried out to the LORD’. The LORD ‘raised up’ a deliverer. The Spirit of the LORD ‘came upon’ him. And ‘the land had rest’ for so many years.

The wheel is held up by mercy. The LORD raises judges because he ‘was moved to pity by their groaning’ (2:18), and he often does it before there is any sign that Israel has truly turned back. In chapter 10 he tells them to go and cry to the gods they have chosen, and yet the scene ends: ‘He could no longer bear the misery of Israel’ (10:16).

But the wheel does not turn in place. It runs downhill. Othniel's story is short and clean. Ehud wins by a trick. Barak will not go to war without Deborah. Gideon begins in fear and ends by making a gold object that ‘became a snare to Gideon and his household’ (8:27). His son Abimelech murders seventy brothers to make himself king. Jephthah makes a vow that costs his daughter, and then leads a slaughter of fellow Israelites. Samson never calls the people to anything and dies alone among his enemies. After Gideon the land is never again said to have rest, and after Samson no judge arises at all.

The way women are treated traces the same slope. The book opens with Acsah, who asks her father for springs of water and receives them (1:12-15), and with Deborah, who leads Israel. It ends with Jephthah's daughter, with the Levite's concubine, and with the young women of Jabesh-gilead and Shiloh, who are never asked and never speak.

The Hebrew word is shophet. In this book it rarely means a judge in a court. It means a leader God raised up to rescue his people and set things right, who often went on to lead a tribe or a region for some years. Chapter 2 puts the two ideas side by side: the LORD raised up judges ‘who saved them’ (2:16).

Some of the judges get full stories. Others get only a notice: a name, a tribe, the number of years, a word about family or wealth, and a burial (10:1-5; 12:8-15). Those short notices speak of quiet years, and they are a reminder that the period was not all war. Deborah is the one judge shown settling cases. She was ‘a prophetess’, and she sat under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, ‘where the Israelites would go up to her for judgment’ (4:4-5).

The book says that the Spirit of the LORD came upon four of the judges: Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson (3:10; 6:34; 11:29; 14:6). The gift was power for a task, and the book is honest that it was not the same thing as good character. The Spirit came on Gideon before he asked for the sign of the fleece, and long before he made his ephod. The Spirit came on Jephthah just before he made his vow. The Spirit came on Samson again and again, and his appetites ruled him to the end. Judges never treats God's gift as approval of what its bearers did with it.

The deliverance is God's, carried out through very human hands. God uses a left-handed man, a woman, a farmer hiding his grain in a winepress, the son of a prostitute, and a man who breaks nearly every vow he carries. None of them is the hero of the book. The LORD is.

parts.h: The deliverers, from Othniel to Samson
parts.body:
Othniel, the nephew of Caleb, is the pattern done right. The Spirit comes on him, he wins, and the land has rest forty years (3:9-11).

Ehud is a left-handed Benjamite who brings Israel's tribute to Eglon, king of Moab, with a short double-edged sword strapped to his right thigh under his cloak. He says he has a secret message for the king, and kills him alone in his upper room (3:15-23). The story is told with irony and some coarse humor at the oppressor's expense, and it is a story of deceit and killing. The text says God raised Ehud up, but it does not say the Spirit came on him, and it does not praise every means he used. Readers have weighed it as an act of war against an occupying king, as a report that leaves the reader to judge the means, or as the first step on the book's slope downward. It is no pattern for anyone today.

Deborah, a prophet, summons Barak to fight Sisera, the commander of a Canaanite king with nine hundred chariots of iron. Barak will not go without her, and she tells him the LORD will sell Sisera ‘into the hand of a woman’ (4:9). The chariots are routed by the River Kishon, and Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael, whose household was at peace with his king. She welcomes him, gives him milk, and kills him with a tent peg while he sleeps. The song in chapter 5 calls her “Most blessed among women” (5:24). Readers have weighed her act in more than one way. Some see a breach of the sacred duty owed to a guest. Some see a woman who chose the side of an oppressed people, at great risk, against a commander who had crushed them for twenty years. Others say the song celebrates the rescue without passing a full judgment on the means. The song ends with Sisera's mother waiting at her window for a son who will not come home, a scene some readers hear as mockery and others as carrying a note of pity.

Gideon is threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding his grain from Midianite raiders, when the angel of the LORD calls him ‘O mighty man of valor’ (6:12). He tears down his father's altar to Baal by night, asks for signs with a fleece, and wins with three hundred men, after God sends the rest home ‘lest Israel glorify themselves over Me’ (7:2). Then the story darkens. He punishes two Israelite towns that would not feed his men, and kills the men of one. He refuses the crown, saying “The LORD shall rule over you” (8:23), but he makes a gold ephod, perhaps a priestly garment, perhaps an object of worship, and all Israel worships it.

His son Abimelech hires men with silver from a temple of Baal and murders his seventy half-brothers ‘on one stone’ (9:5). The leaders of Shechem make him king. After three years king and town turn on each other, and he dies when a woman drops a millstone on his head. The book says plainly that God repaid him (9:56).

Jephthah, driven out by his brothers as the son of a prostitute, is called back to lead Gilead against Ammon. The Spirit comes on him, and then he vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him on his return ‘will belong to the LORD, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering’ (11:31). His only child, his daughter, comes out dancing. Most readers, Jewish and Christian, ancient and modern, have understood that he offered her as a sacrifice. A minority reads the vow as giving her to lifelong service at the sanctuary, unmarried. The chapter note sets out both. On either reading nothing in the book praises the vow, and Scripture elsewhere forbids the sacrifice of children: “You must not worship the LORD your God in this way, because they practice for their gods every abomination which the LORD hates. They even burn their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods” (Deuteronomy 12:31).

Samson is promised to a childless couple of the tribe of Dan, set apart from birth as a Nazirite, and ‘he will begin the deliverance of Israel from the hand of the Philistines’ (13:5). He has great gifts: the Spirit rushes on him, and he tears a lion apart with his bare hands. He has great appetites too. He demands a Philistine wife, goes in to a prostitute at Gaza, and loves Delilah, who sells his secret to the Philistine lords. Shaved, blinded and set to grind grain in prison, he prays once more and pulls down the temple of Dagon, killing more in his death than in his life (16:30). The book gives no verdict on his heart in that last act. It shows only that his prayer was answered.

parts.h: ‘No king in Israel’: the last five chapters
parts.body:
The last five chapters have no judge in them. They tell two stories, and the narrator frames both with one sentence: “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (17:6; 21:25).

In the first, a man named Micah, in the hill country of Ephraim, gives back silver he had stolen from his mother, and she has part of it made into an idol. He sets up a shrine and hires a wandering Levite as his priest, sure that ‘the LORD will be good to me’ (17:13). Then the tribe of Dan, looking for land, takes his idol and his priest, falls on Laish, a town the text twice calls tranquil and unsuspecting, and burns it. They rebuild it as Dan and set up the idol there. The outward forms of Joshua's conquest are all present: the scouts, the report, the attack. What is missing is any word from God beyond a hired priest's vague assurance, and any reason for judgment.

In the second, a Levite and his concubine, a wife of lower standing, stop for the night in Gibeah, a town of Benjamin. Men of the town surround the house and demand the Levite. The old man who has taken them in offers his own daughter and the concubine instead, and the Levite sends his concubine out to the men. They rape and abuse her through the night. At dawn she falls at the door with her hands on the threshold. In the morning he tells her to get up, and there is no answer. He takes her home, cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them through Israel (chapter 19). The tribes demand the guilty men. Benjamin refuses and goes to war, and the tribe is nearly wiped out (chapter 20). Then, to find wives for six hundred survivors, the other tribes destroy the town of Jabesh-gilead and give its four hundred young women to them, and tell the rest to seize young women as they dance at the yearly feast at Shiloh (chapter 21).

These chapters must be read for what they are. The narrator presents them as the depths of Israel's lawlessness, and never as a pattern. The likeness to the story of Sodom in Genesis 19 is deliberate: an Israelite town has become like Sodom. The narrator hardly needs to comment, because the scenes condemn themselves: the woman who never speaks, her hands on the threshold, and the Levite's own account to the tribes, which leaves out what he did (20:4-7).

Any reading that excuses these men, or blames the woman, is a misreading. Whatever had passed between her and the Levite before, nothing in it makes her responsible for what was done to her. The men of Gibeah, the old man and the Levite each answer for what they did, and the text gives none of them a word of defense. Nor does the book approve what Israel did next. A war of revenge nearly destroys a tribe, and the remedy for that disaster is more violence against women. Centuries later Hosea remembered these events as a byword for corruption: ‘They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah’ (Hosea 9:9).

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The refrain invites a question: would a king have saved Israel? Readers have answered in several ways.

Many scholars read the refrain as a case for kings, written in the time of the kings to show why Israel needed one, perhaps David's line in particular. Bethlehem, David's town, appears in these chapters as a place of welcome, and Gibeah, later Saul's hometown, appears at its worst. Others point out that the kings of Israel and Judah often led the people into the same idolatry, as the books of Kings record, so the refrain cannot mean that any king would do. Some read it as a longing for the LORD's own rule, which Gideon had named when he refused the crown: “The LORD shall rule over you” (8:23). Many hold these together. The book shows the chaos of a people without leadership, and the rest of Scripture shows that only a king who rules under God can bring the order they need.

The book has already shown what a bad king looks like. Abimelech made himself king by murder, and his brother Jotham's fable pictures such a king as a thornbush, offering shade and bringing fire (9:8-15).

The next books carry the question on. When the elders ask Samuel for a king ‘like all the other nations’, God tells him, ‘they have rejected Me as their king’ (1 Samuel 8:5, 7), and he gives them one all the same. Samuel and Kings then show some kings who helped and many who made things worse. So Judges does not end with a solution. It ends with a need. A people who forget God are not cured by a stronger ruler.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Judges
parts.body:
The New Testament names the judges only a few times, and it is wise to keep to the lines it draws.

The main one is in Hebrews. After Abraham, Moses and Rahab, the writer runs short of time: “And what more shall I say? Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, and gained what was promised” (Hebrews 11:32-33). Four of those names come from Judges. Hebrews does not praise all they did. It names them because they trusted God, some of them ‘gained strength from weakness’ (Hebrews 11:34), and God worked through them. The point is what God did through people who believed him, not their moral record. That is good news for flawed people, and it is not approval of every act of those named. The list ends by saying that none of them received the promise in full: “God had planned something better for us, so that together with us they would be made perfect” (Hebrews 11:40).

Paul, preaching in Acts, tells Israel's story in a few lines and names the period once: ‘After this, God gave them judges until the time of Samuel the prophet’ (Acts 13:20).

Luke's first chapter echoes the book twice. John the Baptist is never to take wine or strong drink (Luke 1:15), as Samson's mother was told before his birth (13:4-5). And when Elizabeth greets Mary with “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:42), her words recall Deborah's song: “Most blessed among women is Jael” (5:24). Mary, too, is a woman through whom God rescues his people, but by giving birth and not by a sword.

Judges does not foretell Christ, and these notes do not make any judge a picture of him. What the book shows is the need. Each judge saved Israel ‘while the judge was still alive’ (2:18), and each rest ended at a grave.

Judges is Israel's Scripture first, and it records Israel's failures as honestly as Israel's own prophets did. Nothing in it, or in the New Testament's use of it, is a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people.

A few habits will help a new reader.

Read chapter 2 slowly. It is the key to the middle of the book, and every story after it is another turn of the same wheel.

Watch the refrains. The narrator rarely stops to say what to think, but the repeated phrases are the book's own comment: who did evil, who cried out, who was raised up, how long the land had rest. Notice too when the refrains stop. After Gideon the land never has rest again, and in the last chapters there is no judge at all.

Do not take the judges as models. Telling what someone did is not the same as recommending it. The book shows its judgment through what follows an act, through the law of Moses that stands behind the whole story, and above all through its last sentence. Even the people Hebrews names for their faith are not held up for everything they did.

Do not skip the hard chapters, and do not read them alone. The chapter notes take them one at a time, say plainly what happens, and set out how careful readers have weighed them. None of those readings makes them painless.

Do not carry the book into the present as a program. Its wars name peoples who passed away long ago. It gives no nation, no church and no person a warrant for violence against anyone.

And read Ruth after it. Ruth is set in the same dark years, in a small town, and shows what faithfulness looked like when everyone else was doing what was right in his own eyes. Judges ends with no king. Ruth ends with the name of the king to come: ‘Jesse was the father of David’ (Ruth 4:22).

hard.line: Adoni-bezek's thumbs and big toes: the cruelty of the age, and the captured king's own verdict on it.
The LORD was with Judah, yet the iron chariots stayed: two ways of reading the chapter's failures.
Why the nations were left in the land: judgment, and a test.
Ehud and Eglon: an assassination by a trick, and how readers have weighed the means.
Jael and Sisera: a guest's trust broken, and how readers have weighed her act.
The song's praise of Jael, and Sisera's mother at the window.
The fleece: a way to seek guidance, or weak faith met by God's patience?
Gideon's revenge on Succoth and Penuel: a deliverer turning on his own people.
Gideon refuses the crown, then makes an ephod that becomes a snare.
Abimelech murders his seventy brothers to make himself king.
God sends a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and Shechem: what the words mean.
Jephthah's vow and his daughter: the two main readings, and why nothing here praises the vow.
Shibboleth: men of Israel killed at the fords for the way they spoke.
‘This was from the LORD’: God at work through Samson's wrong choices.
Samson's death: the ways readers have understood his last act and his prayer.
The Danites destroy a tranquil town: the forms of conquest without God's word.
The Levite's concubine: what was done to her, and why no reading may excuse the men or blame her.
Israel asks God about a war on Benjamin, and loses twice: a war among brothers.
The young women of Jabesh-gilead and Shiloh, taken without being asked, and the book's last verdict.

words.line: The Hebrew shophet: a leader God raised up to rescue his people and set things right, more often a deliverer than a judge in court (2:16).
The Berean Standard Bible's word for someone God raised up to save Israel from an enemy (3:9, 3:15).
Baal was the storm god of Canaan, believed to bring the rain and the harvest. ‘The Baals’ are his local forms and shrines (2:11).
Goddesses worshiped beside Baal. Israel served them too (2:13; 3:7).
Israel's cry to God in distress, which again and again moved him to send help (3:9; 10:10).
The years of peace after a deliverance: forty, eighty, forty and forty (3:11; 3:30; 5:31; 8:28). After Gideon the land is never again said to have rest.

words.word: The Spirit of the LORD came upon
words.line: God's power given to a judge for a task. The book never mistakes the gift for good character (3:10; 14:6).
A garment worn by priests and used in seeking God's guidance. Gideon's gold ephod became a thing Israel worshiped (8:27).
A person set apart to God by a vow: no wine, no razor, no touching the dead (Numbers 6). Samson was one from the womb (13:5).
The word the men of Gilead used at the fords to tell an Ephraimite by his speech (12:6).
A member of the tribe of Levi, set apart for service at the sanctuary and given towns instead of a share of land (17:7).
A wife of lower standing, bound to a man but without the full place of a first wife (19:1).
Small figures kept in a home and perhaps used to seek guidance, called teraphim in Hebrew. Micah kept them in his shrine (17:5).
The words that open the last chapters, with the refrain that there was no king in Israel (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25).

timeline.when: About 1375 to 1050 BC, or about 1200 to 1050 BC
timeline.what: The two main spans proposed for the judges. Which is right depends on the date of the exodus.
The monument of Pharaoh Merneptah names a people called Israel living in Canaan.
The great powers of the Late Bronze Age collapse, and Egypt's hold on Canaan weakens.
More than 250 small villages appear in the central hill country, most of them on hilltops.
The Philistines settle on the southern coast. Reliefs of Ramesses III name the Peleset among the Sea Peoples.
The tribes fight for their land and leave many Canaanite towns standing (chapter 1). A new generation does not know the LORD (2:10).
Cushan-rishathaim rules over Israel. Othniel delivers them, and the land has rest (3:8-11).
Jabin and Sisera oppress Israel. Deborah, Barak and Jael (chapters 4 and 5).
Midian's raids, and Gideon (chapters 6 to 8). Abimelech rules three years after him (9:22).
The Philistines rule over Israel (13:1). Samson judges twenty years in the days of the Philistines (15:20).
The two closing stories. Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, serves before the ark, which places the war with Benjamin early in the period (20:28).
The Song of Deborah, widely held to be one of the oldest Hebrew poems, perhaps composed not long after the battle (chapter 5).
The Assyrian deportations from northern Israel begin, which many take to be ‘the captivity of the land’ in 18:30.
Hebrews names Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah among those who acted by faith (Hebrews 11:32).
Martin Noth proposes that the books from Deuteronomy to Kings form one history, Judges among them.

places.name: Shechem
places.line: Abimelech's mother's town, whose leaders made him king and whom he later destroyed (chapter 9).

places.name: Bethel
places.line: Deborah judged Israel between Ramah and Bethel (4:5). In the war with Benjamin the tribes went up to Bethel to ask God (20:18).

places.name: Jericho
places.line: The City of Palms, Jericho or its oasis, which Eglon of Moab took and held for eighteen years (3:13-14).

places.name: The Jordan
places.line: At its fords Ehud's men cut off Moab (3:28), and the men of Gilead stopped the Ephraimites with the word Shibboleth (12:5-6).

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Called Jebus, and still held by the Jebusites (1:21). The Levite would not stay the night there among foreigners (19:10-12).

places.name: Bethlehem
places.line: Home of the young Levite who became Micah's priest (17:7) and of the Levite's concubine (19:1).

places.name: Hebron
places.line: Taken by Judah and given to Caleb (1:10, 1:20). Samson carried the gates of Gaza to a hill facing it (16:3).

places.name: Gilead
places.line: The land east of the Jordan: Jair's towns, Jephthah's home, and Jabesh-gilead (10:3-4; 11:1; 21:8). Drawn roughly.

teaching.mapNote: Only eight places are drawn, each placed elsewhere on this site. Hazor, Tabor, Jezreel, Ophrah, Shiloh, Gibeah, Mizpah, Dan and the Philistine towns are left off, because where they lay is debated or is not placed in this site's records. No tribal borders are drawn. The map shows the story's places and makes no claim about any border today.
